general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.t: Gross Specimen: Coagulative Necrosis of Myocardium
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.sc: A gross heart specimen shows a pale, yellow-tan, wedge-shaped area in the anterior left ventricular wall with preserved tissue architecture on cut section, sent from a patient who died 3 days after chest pain.
tk: Identify the type of necrosis shown in the specimen.
Name the most likely underlying cause of this lesion.
State one histological feature that would confirm this diagnosis under the microscope.
Name one serum cardiac biomarker that would be elevated in this condition.
ck: Correctly identifies coagulative necrosis
States acute myocardial infarction due to coronary artery occlusion
Describes preserved cell outlines with loss of nuclei (karyolysis) on microscopy
Names troponin I/T or CK-MB as an elevated biomarker

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.sc: A photomicrograph of brain tissue shows an area of tissue softening and cystic cavitation with macrophage infiltration, taken from a patient who had a cerebral infarct two weeks earlier.
tk: Identify the type of necrosis shown.
Explain why the brain characteristically undergoes this type of necrosis rather than coagulative necrosis.
Name the predominant cell type responsible for clearing the necrotic debris.
State the eventual gross outcome of this lesion if the patient survives.
ck: Identifies liquefactive necrosis
Explains high lipid content and lack of substantial structural (collagen) framework in brain tissue
Names microglia/macrophages as the clearing cells
States formation of a fluid-filled cystic cavity

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.sc: A chest X-ray and a lymph node biopsy are shown from a patient with chronic cough and weight loss. The biopsy shows granulomas with central, structureless, cheese-like eosinophilic material.
tk: Identify the type of necrosis illustrated.
Name the most likely causative organism.
Name the characteristic special stain used to identify this organism.
Name the type of hypersensitivity reaction responsible for granuloma formation.
ck: Identifies caseous necrosis
Names Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Names Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) stain
States Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.t: Gross Specimen: Dry Gangrene of the Foot
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.sc: A photograph shows a diabetic patient's foot with a well-demarcated, dry, black, shriveled great toe, with a clear line of separation from adjacent viable tissue.
tk: Identify the type of gangrene shown and justify using the described features.
Name the underlying vascular pathology most commonly responsible for this condition in a diabetic patient.
Differentiate this condition from wet gangrene in terms of bacterial infection.
State the definitive surgical management typically required.
ck: Identifies dry gangrene, citing dry, shriveled, well-demarcated appearance
Names atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease/diabetic microangiopathy
States dry gangrene has minimal/no superimposed bacterial infection, unlike wet gangrene
States amputation at an appropriate level

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.sc: A resected appendix specimen is shown, appearing swollen, congested, and covered with a fibrinopurulent exudate on its serosal surface.
tk: Name the type of inflammation shown.
List two cardinal cellular mediators/cells responsible for the acute inflammatory response.
Name the vascular change responsible for the swelling seen.
State one possible serious complication if this condition is untreated.
ck: Identifies acute (fibrinopurulent) inflammation
Names neutrophils and mediators such as histamine/prostaglandins
States increased vascular permeability causing exudation/edema
States perforation with peritonitis as a complication

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.sc: A photomicrograph from a healing surgical wound (day 7) shows numerous small proliferating capillaries, fibroblasts, and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate.
tk: Identify the tissue shown.
Name the two principal cell types responsible for forming this tissue.
Name the process by which new capillaries form in this tissue.
State whether this pattern of repair represents primary or secondary intention healing, and justify.
ck: Identifies granulation tissue
Names fibroblasts and endothelial cells
Names angiogenesis
Identifies healing by primary intention if wound edges are apposed, or explains reasoning

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.sc: An X-ray of the tibia shows a sequestrum (dead bone fragment) surrounded by a thickened involucrum, in a patient with a discharging sinus for six months.
tk: Define the terms 'sequestrum' and 'involucrum'.
Name the most common causative organism of pyogenic osteomyelitis.
State the type of inflammation present in this chronic condition.
Name one long-term complication that can arise from chronic sinus discharge.
ck: Defines sequestrum as dead bone and involucrum as new bone formed around it
Names Staphylococcus aureus
States chronic (suppurative) inflammation
States squamous cell carcinoma (Marjolin's ulcer) as a long-term complication

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.sc: A hysterectomy specimen shows multiple well-circumscribed, firm, whorled, gray-white nodules within the myometrium.
tk: Identify whether this tumor is benign or malignant, and justify using gross features.
Name the tissue of origin of this tumor.
State the suffix used to name a benign tumor of smooth muscle origin.
Name one clinical symptom this tumor commonly causes.
ck: Identifies benign tumor, citing well-circumscribed borders and whorled pattern
Names smooth muscle (myometrium) as the tissue of origin
States the suffix '-oma' (leiomyoma)
States menorrhagia or pelvic pressure/mass symptoms

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.t: Photomicrograph: Squamous Cell Carcinoma with Keratin Pearls
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.sc: A photomicrograph from a skin biopsy shows irregular nests of atypical squamous cells invading the dermis, with whorled keratin pearl formation and marked nuclear pleomorphism.
tk: Identify the tumor shown.
Define 'keratin pearl' and state its significance.
List two histological features of malignancy visible in this specimen.
Name the most important risk factor for this tumor at this site.
ck: Identifies squamous cell carcinoma
Defines keratin pearl as concentric whorls of keratinizing squamous cells, indicating differentiation
Lists nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and/or invasion
Names chronic UV (sun) exposure

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.sc: A 55-year-old man presents with elevated serum PSA and a hard prostatic nodule on digital rectal examination.
tk: Name the tumor marker used in this scenario and the organ it is associated with.
State one important limitation of using this marker alone for diagnosis.
Name the gold-standard diagnostic procedure required to confirm malignancy.
Name the grading system specifically used for prostate cancer.
ck: Names PSA associated with prostate
States PSA can be elevated in benign prostatic hyperplasia/prostatitis (lack of specificity)
States transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy
Names the Gleason grading system

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.sc: A cut section of liver shows multiple well-demarcated, pale, umbilicated nodules of varying sizes scattered throughout both lobes.
tk: State whether this pattern represents a primary or secondary liver tumor, and justify.
Name the term used for central umbilication/depression seen in some metastatic nodules.
Name two common primary sites for liver metastasis.
Name the most common route of spread of tumor to the liver from a gastrointestinal primary.
ck: Identifies metastatic (secondary) tumor, citing multiple discrete nodules
Explains umbilication is due to central necrosis
Names colon, lung, breast, stomach or pancreas as common primaries
States portal venous spread from GI tract primaries

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.t: Peripheral Blood Film: Iron Deficiency Anemia
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.sc: A peripheral blood film shows microcytic, hypochromic red cells with increased central pallor and anisopoikilocytosis.
tk: Identify the type of anemia illustrated.
Name two laboratory iron study findings expected in this condition.
Name one common cause of this condition in an adult male.
State the first-line treatment for this condition.
ck: Identifies iron deficiency (microcytic hypochromic) anemia
States low serum ferritin/iron and high TIBC
States chronic gastrointestinal blood loss as a cause
States oral iron replacement therapy

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.t: Peripheral Blood Film: Sickle Cell Disease
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.sc: A peripheral blood film from a young patient with recurrent bone pain shows numerous crescent-shaped red blood cells along with target cells and Howell-Jolly bodies.
tk: Identify the abnormal cells shown and the diagnosis they suggest.
Explain the underlying molecular defect causing this condition.
Explain the significance of Howell-Jolly bodies in this blood film.
Name one precipitating factor for a vaso-occlusive crisis.
ck: Identifies sickle cells, diagnosis of sickle cell disease
Explains a point mutation causing glutamate to valine substitution in beta-globin (HbS)
Explains Howell-Jolly bodies indicate functional hyposplenism/asplenia
States hypoxia, dehydration, infection, or cold as a precipitant

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.sc: A peripheral blood film from a child with fever, pallor, and bruising shows numerous large blast cells with high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio and scant cytoplasm.
tk: Identify the general diagnosis suggested by this blood film.
Name the special stain that would help distinguish acute lymphoblastic from acute myeloid leukemia.
State the significance of a positive Auer rod finding on the blast cells.
Name one common presenting symptom explained by bone marrow failure in this condition.
ck: Identifies acute leukemia
Names myeloperoxidase (MPO) stain
States Auer rods indicate myeloid lineage (AML)
States anemia (pallor/fatigue), bleeding (thrombocytopenia), or infection (neutropenia)

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.sc: A lymph node biopsy photomicrograph shows a large binucleate cell with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli resembling 'owl's eyes,' surrounded by a mixed inflammatory background.
tk: Identify the cell shown and its diagnostic significance.
Name the disease in which this cell is considered pathognomonic.
Name the immunohistochemical marker typically positive on this cell.
State the general prognosis of this disease compared to non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
ck: Identifies Reed-Sternberg cell
Names Hodgkin lymphoma
Names CD15 and/or CD30 positivity
States generally more favorable/curable prognosis with modern therapy

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.sc: An opened aorta specimen shows multiple raised, yellow, lipid-laden plaques with some areas of ulceration and calcification along the intimal surface.
tk: Identify the pathological process shown.
Name the earliest grossly visible lesion in this disease process (precursor to the plaque).
Name two major modifiable risk factors for this condition.
State one major clinical complication of plaque rupture.
ck: Identifies atherosclerosis
Names the fatty streak as the earliest lesion
Names hypertension, smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia, or obesity
States thrombosis leading to myocardial infarction or stroke

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.sc: A photomicrograph of myocardium from a patient with a history of recurrent sore throats shows a nodular focus of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by lymphocytes and large activated macrophages (Anitschkow cells).
tk: Identify the structure shown and the disease it indicates.
Name the preceding infection responsible for triggering this disease.
Explain the immunological mechanism underlying this disease.
Name the valve most commonly and severely affected in the chronic phase.
ck: Identifies Aschoff body, diagnosis of rheumatic heart disease
Names prior Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) pharyngitis
Explains molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens and cardiac tissue
Names the mitral valve

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.sc: A CT scan and gross lung specimen show consolidation of an entire lobe with a firm, gray, granular cut surface in a patient with high fever and productive cough.
tk: Identify the pathological process and its typical stage based on the gray, firm appearance.
Name the most common causative organism of community-acquired lobar pneumonia.
List the four classical pathological stages of lobar pneumonia in order.
State one major complication if the infection is not adequately treated.
ck: Identifies lobar pneumonia at the grey hepatization stage
Names Streptococcus pneumoniae
Lists congestion, red hepatization, grey hepatization, resolution in order
States lung abscess, empyema, or organization/fibrosis as a complication

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.sc: A photomicrograph of lung tissue from a long-term smoker shows destruction of alveolar walls with abnormal permanent enlargement of air spaces, predominantly affecting the respiratory bronchioles.
tk: Identify the condition shown.
Name the enzyme-protease imbalance implicated in its pathogenesis.
Name the genetic condition associated with a panacinar pattern of this disease.
State the classic clinical body habitus term associated with this condition.
ck: Identifies centriacinar (centrilobular) emphysema
Names protease (elastase)-antiprotease (alpha-1 antitrypsin) imbalance
Names alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
States 'pink puffer' body habitus

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.sc: A gross lung specimen shows a large, dark red, coiled thrombus lodged at the bifurcation of the pulmonary artery (a saddle embolus).
tk: Identify the finding and state its most common source/origin.
Name the clinical triad of risk factors predisposing to this condition (Virchow's triad).
State the most severe immediate clinical consequence of a large saddle embolus.
Name one investigation used to confirm this diagnosis clinically.
ck: Identifies pulmonary thromboembolism, originating typically from deep leg veins
Names Virchow's triad: stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial injury
States sudden death from acute right heart failure/cardiogenic shock
States CT pulmonary angiography or D-dimer with imaging

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.sc: A graph is shown plotting the dose-response curves of Drug X and Drug Y, where Drug Y's curve lies to the right of Drug X's curve but both reach the same maximal effect (Emax).
tk: State which drug is more potent and justify your answer using the graph.
Define 'potency' as illustrated by this graph.
State whether the two drugs differ in efficacy, and justify.
Name one clinical scenario where potency differences between two similar drugs are clinically important.
ck: Identifies Drug X as more potent (lower dose for same effect)
Defines potency as the dose required to produce a given effect
States efficacy is equal since both reach the same Emax
Gives a reasonable example such as opioid dosing equivalence

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.sc: A semi-logarithmic plasma concentration versus time graph for a drug shows a straight line, and the student is told the drug has a half-life of 4 hours.
tk: Identify the type of elimination kinetics illustrated by this straight-line semi-log plot.
Calculate the approximate percentage of drug remaining after 3 half-lives (12 hours).
State how the elimination rate constant (k) relates to the half-life.
Contrast this pattern with zero-order kinetics using one example drug that follows zero-order kinetics.
ck: Identifies first-order kinetics
Correctly calculates approximately 12.5% remaining after 3 half-lives
States k = 0.693/t1/2
Names a zero-order drug such as ethanol, phenytoin (at high doses), or aspirin (in overdose)

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.sc: A patient on digoxin therapy presents with nausea, visual disturbances, and arrhythmia; serum digoxin level is markedly elevated above the therapeutic range.
tk: Define 'therapeutic index' and explain its relevance to this scenario.
State why digoxin specifically requires therapeutic drug monitoring.
Name the specific antidote available for severe digoxin toxicity.
Name one electrolyte disturbance that predisposes to digoxin toxicity.
ck: Defines therapeutic index as the ratio of toxic dose to effective dose, notes digoxin has a narrow index
States narrow therapeutic index necessitates monitoring
Names digoxin immune Fab (antidigoxin antibody fragments)
States hypokalemia (or hypomagnesemia/hypercalcemia) predisposes to toxicity

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.sc: A pharmacological diagram shows Drug A binding reversibly to a receptor, and adding increasing doses of Drug B (a competitive antagonist) shifts Drug A's dose-response curve to the right without lowering the maximal effect.
tk: Classify Drug B's mechanism of antagonism illustrated in this diagram.
State how the curve would differ if Drug B were a non-competitive (irreversible) antagonist instead.
Define 'agonist' as it applies to Drug A.
Name one clinically used competitive antagonist and its receptor target.
ck: Identifies competitive antagonism (parallel rightward shift, same Emax)
States non-competitive antagonism would reduce Emax without full rightward shift reversal at high dose
Defines agonist as a drug that binds and activates a receptor to produce a response
Names an example such as naloxone at opioid receptors or atropine at muscarinic receptors

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.sc: A critically ill patient requires rapid achievement of a therapeutic plasma concentration of a drug with a large volume of distribution; the clinician decides to administer a loading dose rather than relying on maintenance dosing alone.
tk: State the formula used to calculate a loading dose.
Explain why a loading dose achieves therapeutic concentration faster than starting with a maintenance dose alone.
Name one factor that would require downward adjustment of a loading dose in a specific patient population.
State how maintenance dose calculation differs conceptually from loading dose calculation.
ck: States Loading dose = (Target plasma concentration x Volume of distribution) / Bioavailability
Explains a loading dose rapidly fills the volume of distribution to reach target concentration without waiting through multiple half-lives
Names reduced volume of distribution or altered protein binding (e.g., in edema, obesity, renal/hepatic impairment) as a factor
States maintenance dose depends on clearance and desired steady-state concentration, not volume of distribution

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.sc: A farmworker presents with excessive salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhea, miosis, bradycardia, and muscle fasciculations after exposure to a pesticide.
tk: Identify the toxidrome and the likely causative class of agent.
Name the two drugs used in the standard antidotal treatment of this poisoning.
Explain the mechanism of action of the first antidote named.
State why atropine alone is insufficient to fully treat this poisoning.
ck: Identifies cholinergic toxidrome from organophosphate poisoning
Names atropine and pralidoxime (2-PAM)
Explains atropine as a competitive muscarinic receptor antagonist
States atropine does not reactivate acetylcholinesterase or address nicotinic effects (muscle weakness/fasciculations)

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.sc: A patient with hypertension and coexisting asthma requires beta-blocker therapy for cardiovascular protection; the physician selects a cardioselective agent.
tk: Name two examples of cardioselective (beta-1 selective) beta-blockers.
Explain why a non-selective beta-blocker (e.g., propranolol) would be relatively contraindicated in this patient.
Name one important caution regarding cardioselectivity at higher doses.
Name one other important contraindication to beta-blocker use unrelated to asthma.
ck: Names metoprolol and/or atenolol (or bisoprolol)
Explains beta-2 blockade can cause bronchoconstriction, worsening asthma
States cardioselectivity is relative and lost at higher doses
States severe bradycardia, heart block, or decompensated heart failure as another contraindication

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.sc: A patient in anaphylactic shock requires immediate pharmacological treatment with an agent that has combined alpha-1, beta-1, and beta-2 agonist activity.
tk: Name the drug of choice in this scenario.
Explain the therapeutic benefit of its alpha-1 agonist activity in anaphylaxis.
Explain the therapeutic benefit of its beta-2 agonist activity in anaphylaxis.
Name the preferred route and site of administration in an emergency setting.
ck: Names epinephrine (adrenaline)
States alpha-1 activity causes vasoconstriction, reversing hypotension and mucosal edema
States beta-2 activity causes bronchodilation, relieving bronchospasm
States intramuscular injection into the anterolateral thigh

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.sc: A hypertensive patient started on lisinopril develops a persistent dry cough and, in a separate visit, presents with facial and lip swelling.
tk: Explain the mechanism responsible for the dry cough associated with this drug class.
Name the serious adverse effect represented by the facial/lip swelling.
Name the alternative drug class that can be used with a lower risk of both these adverse effects.
State one important contraindication to ACE inhibitor use in pregnancy.
ck: Explains accumulation of bradykinin due to ACE inhibition causing cough
Identifies angioedema
Names angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs)
States ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetotoxicity/teratogenicity

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.sc: A patient on long-term warfarin therapy for atrial fibrillation requires routine monitoring, and the report shows an INR of 6.5 with mild gum bleeding.
tk: Name the laboratory test used to monitor warfarin therapy.
Explain the mechanism of action of warfarin.
Name the reversal agent(s) used for significant warfarin-associated bleeding.
Name one common drug interaction that can potentiate warfarin's effect.
ck: Names INR (International Normalized Ratio) based on prothrombin time
Explains inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X
Names vitamin K and/or fresh frozen plasma/prothrombin complex concentrate
Names an interacting drug such as aspirin, metronidazole, or amiodarone

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.sc: A patient on high-dose atorvastatin presents with diffuse muscle pain and dark urine; laboratory tests reveal markedly elevated creatine kinase.
tk: Name the serious adverse effect suggested by these findings.
Explain the mechanism of action of statins in lowering cholesterol.
Name one drug interaction that increases the risk of this adverse effect.
State the appropriate immediate management step regarding the statin.
ck: Identifies rhabdomyolysis (statin-induced myopathy)
Explains HMG-CoA reductase inhibition, reducing hepatic cholesterol synthesis and upregulating LDL receptors
Names an interacting drug such as fibrates, macrolides, or grapefruit juice (CYP3A4 inhibitors)
States discontinuation of the statin and supportive care/hydration

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/antimi.sc: A patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis) requires antibiotic treatment for a serious infection typically treated with a beta-lactam.
tk: Explain the mechanism of action shared by penicillins and cephalosporins.
State the approximate cross-reactivity risk between penicillins and cephalosporins in a patient with true penicillin allergy.
Name a class of antibiotic that can be safely used as an alternative in this patient with minimal cross-reactivity concern.
Name one non-beta-lactam alternative used for serious Gram-positive infections.
ck: Explains inhibition of bacterial cell wall (peptidoglycan) synthesis via penicillin-binding proteins
States a relatively low but existing cross-reactivity risk (especially with first-generation cephalosporins)
Names macrolides, fluoroquinolones, or aztreonam (for severe allergy) as alternatives
Names vancomycin or clindamycin

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/antimi.sc: A patient on gentamicin therapy for a serious Gram-negative infection requires monitoring of peak and trough drug levels.
tk: Name the two major organ toxicities requiring monitoring with aminoglycoside therapy.
Explain why trough levels are specifically monitored in this drug class.
Name one other drug class that potentiates ototoxicity when combined with aminoglycosides.
State the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides.
ck: Names nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity
Explains high trough levels indicate inadequate clearance and risk of toxic accumulation
Names loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) as potentiating ototoxicity
States irreversible binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA and inhibiting protein synthesis

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/antimi.sc: A patient on standard four-drug anti-tuberculosis therapy develops peripheral neuropathy (numbness and tingling in the feet).
tk: Identify which anti-tuberculosis drug is most likely responsible for this adverse effect.
Explain the mechanism by which this drug causes the described adverse effect.
Name the vitamin supplement used to prevent/treat this adverse effect.
Name one other major adverse effect associated with a different first-line anti-tuberculosis drug.
ck: Identifies isoniazid
Explains isoniazid interferes with pyridoxine (vitamin B6) metabolism/increases its excretion
Names pyridoxine (vitamin B6)
Names hepatotoxicity (isoniazid/rifampicin/pyrazinamide), optic neuritis (ethambutol), or orange body fluid discoloration (rifampicin)

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/antimi.sc: A patient with systemic candidiasis is treated with an intravenous antifungal agent known for causing significant nephrotoxicity and infusion-related fever/chills ('shake and bake' reaction).
tk: Identify the antifungal drug being described.
Explain its mechanism of action against fungal cells.
Name a newer lipid-based formulation strategy used to reduce this drug's toxicity.
Name an alternative, less nephrotoxic class of antifungal drugs used for similar indications.
ck: Identifies amphotericin B
Explains binding to ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane, forming pores that increase permeability
Names liposomal amphotericin B formulations
Names azoles (e.g., fluconazole, voriconazole) or echinocandins

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cns-ph.sc: A patient is brought to the emergency department with drowsiness, slurred speech, and respiratory depression after an intentional overdose of diazepam tablets.
tk: Name the specific antidote used for benzodiazepine overdose.
Explain the mechanism of action of benzodiazepines at the GABA-A receptor.
State one important precaution regarding use of the antidote in a chronic benzodiazepine user.
Name one non-pharmacological supportive measure important in managing this overdose.
ck: Names flumazenil
Explains benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A receptor chloride channel opening frequency, potentiating inhibitory neurotransmission
States flumazenil can precipitate withdrawal seizures in chronic users/dependence
States airway support/ventilatory support as needed

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cns-ph.sc: A young woman with epilepsy who is planning pregnancy is currently on sodium valproate for seizure control.
tk: Name the major teratogenic risk associated with valproate use during pregnancy.
State the recommended supplementation that reduces the risk of this defect.
Name one antiepileptic drug generally considered to have a more favorable safety profile in pregnancy.
State why abrupt discontinuation of an antiepileptic drug is generally avoided.
ck: Names neural tube defects (e.g., spina bifida)
States high-dose folic acid supplementation
Names lamotrigine or levetiracetam as relatively safer alternatives
States risk of precipitating status epilepticus/withdrawal seizures

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cns-ph.sc: A patient on long-term haloperidol therapy develops fever, muscle rigidity, autonomic instability, and altered mental status.
tk: Identify the life-threatening syndrome described.
Name the class of drugs most commonly responsible for this syndrome.
Name the first-line pharmacological treatment for this syndrome.
Name one other important extrapyramidal adverse effect associated with typical antipsychotics.
ck: Identifies neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Names typical (first-generation) antipsychotics
Names dantrolene and/or bromocriptine
Names acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, or tardive dyskinesia

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cns-ph.sc: A postoperative patient requires opioid analgesia; the physician must select between morphine and a synthetic opioid with a shorter duration of action for procedural sedation.
tk: Name a short-acting synthetic opioid commonly used for procedural sedation.
Name the receptor primarily responsible for opioid analgesia and respiratory depression.
Name the antidote used for opioid-induced respiratory depression.
State one common gastrointestinal adverse effect of chronic opioid use.
ck: Names fentanyl (or remifentanil)
Names the mu (μ) opioid receptor
Names naloxone
States constipation

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cns-ph.t: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor (SSRI) Interaction Station
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cns-ph.sc: A patient on fluoxetine for depression is started on tramadol for pain and subsequently develops agitation, hyperthermia, tremor, and hyperreflexia.
tk: Identify the syndrome suggested by these findings.
Explain the pharmacological mechanism responsible for this interaction.
Name one other class of drugs that can precipitate this syndrome when combined with an SSRI.
State the general management approach for this syndrome.
ck: Identifies serotonin syndrome
Explains excessive serotonergic activity from combined serotonin reuptake inhibition and additional serotonergic effect (tramadol)
Names monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or other serotonergic agents
States discontinuation of offending drugs, supportive care, and cyproheptadine (serotonin antagonist) if needed

microbiology-and-immunology/general-bact.sc: A photomicrograph of a Gram-stained sputum smear shows Gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci arranged in pairs.
tk: Identify the most likely organism shown.
Name the disease most commonly caused by this organism in the respiratory tract.
Name the culture medium and characteristic colony finding (e.g., alpha-hemolysis) used to identify this organism.
Name the vaccine available to prevent infection with this organism.
ck: Identifies Streptococcus pneumoniae
Names lobar pneumonia
States blood agar with alpha-hemolytic (green) colonies, optochin-sensitive
Names the pneumococcal conjugate or polysaccharide vaccine

microbiology-and-immunology/general-bact.sc: A MacConkey agar plate inoculated with a stool sample shows pink (lactose-fermenting) colonies.
tk: Explain the principle behind color differentiation on this medium.
Name two lactose-fermenting organisms that could produce pink colonies here.
Name one non-lactose fermenting enteric pathogen that would appear pale/colorless on this medium.
State the selective component of this medium and its purpose.
ck: Explains lactose fermentation with pH indicator changing color to pink
Names E. coli and/or Klebsiella species
Names Salmonella or Shigella species
States bile salts selectively inhibit Gram-positive organisms

microbiology-and-immunology/general-bact.sc: A patient presents with a sore throat, a thick grey pseudomembrane over the tonsils, and signs of myocarditis.
tk: Identify the most likely causative organism.
Name the toxin responsible for the systemic manifestations (e.g., myocarditis).
Name the laboratory test used to confirm toxin production by the isolate.
Name the preventive vaccine component targeting this organism's toxin.
ck: Identifies Corynebacterium diphtheriae
Names diphtheria toxin
Names the Elek test
Names the diphtheria toxoid (as in DPT/pentavalent vaccine)

microbiology-and-immunology/general-bact.sc: A Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion plate is shown with a bacterial lawn and several antibiotic disks, some showing large clear zones of inhibition and others showing no zone.
tk: Explain what a large zone of inhibition indicates about the organism's susceptibility.
Name the reference standard used to interpret zone diameters as susceptible, intermediate, or resistant.
State one limitation of the disk diffusion method compared to the E-test.
Name the test used to determine the minimum inhibitory concentration precisely.
ck: States a large zone indicates susceptibility to that antibiotic
Names CLSI (Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute) breakpoints
States disk diffusion gives categorical results, not a precise MIC value
Names the E-test (epsilometer test) or broth microdilution

microbiology-and-immunology/general-bact.sc: A patient develops a deep wound infection with crepitus (gas in tissue), severe pain out of proportion to examination findings, and a foul-smelling discharge following a traumatic injury.
tk: Identify the most likely causative organism class and specific genus.
Name the toxin responsible for the severe muscle necrosis seen in this condition.
Name the classic surgical management required in addition to antibiotics.
State whether this organism is Gram-positive or Gram-negative and whether it is spore-forming.
ck: Identifies Clostridium (gas gangrene, e.g., Clostridium perfringens)
Names alpha-toxin (a lecithinase/phospholipase)
States urgent surgical debridement
States Gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobic bacillus

microbiology-and-immunology/virology.sc: A patient's hepatitis B serology panel shows HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgM positive, and anti-HBs negative.
tk: Interpret this serological pattern in terms of the stage of infection.
Name the marker that indicates high infectivity if positive in this patient.
State the expected serology pattern of a person who has been successfully vaccinated against hepatitis B.

Name one live attenuated vaccine given in the routine schedule and one contraindication to its use.
State the purpose of a 'catch-up' immunization schedule.
ck: Names pentavalent (DPT-HepB-Hib), OPV, and/or pneumococcal conjugate vaccine as appropriate for this age
Explains maintaining proper vaccine temperature from manufacture to administration to preserve potency
Names OPV or BCG as live vaccines; states contraindication in severe immunodeficiency
States it allows children who missed doses to complete the required vaccine series appropriately

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.t: Nutrition Program Station: Vitamin A Supplementation
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.sc: A national child health program provides periodic high-dose vitamin A supplementation to children aged 6 months to 5 years.
tk: State the primary public health objectives of this vitamin A supplementation program.
Name the ocular condition that vitamin A deficiency can cause if left untreated.
Explain the mechanism by which vitamin A supplementation reduces mortality from infections such as measles.
Name one other major micronutrient deficiency disorder targeted by a similar national supplementation/fortification program.
ck: States reducing child mortality/morbidity from infections and preventing vitamin A deficiency-related blindness
Names xerophthalmia (leading to blindness)
Explains improved immune function/epithelial integrity reducing infection severity
Names iodine deficiency (salt iodization) or iron deficiency (anemia prevention)

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.sc: A rural community relies on an open well for drinking water located near a cattle shed and experiences recurrent outbreaks of diarrheal disease.
tk: Identify the most likely mode of contamination responsible for the recurrent outbreaks.
Name the single most effective long-term public health intervention to address this problem.
Name one simple household-level water treatment method that could reduce risk in the interim.
Name the water quality indicator organism commonly tested to assess fecal contamination.
ck: Identifies fecal contamination of the well water from nearby animal waste
States provision of safe water supply and proper sanitation infrastructure
States boiling, chlorination, or filtration of household water
Names E. coli (or total/fecal coliforms) as the indicator organism

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.sc: A 50-year-old man who has worked for 25 years in a stone-quarrying industry presents with progressive shortness of breath, and chest X-ray shows diffuse nodular opacities predominantly in the upper lung zones.
tk: Identify the most likely occupational lung disease.
Name the specific causative agent responsible for this condition.
Name the hierarchy of control measure considered most effective for preventing this disease at the source.
Name one other occupational lung disease caused by a different specific dust, along with its associated occupation.
ck: Identifies silicosis
Names crystalline silica dust
States elimination/substitution of the hazard (e.g., wet drilling methods, dust suppression) as most effective, following the hierarchy of controls
Names asbestosis (asbestos, construction/insulation workers), byssinosis (cotton dust, textile workers), or coal workers' pneumoconiosis (coal dust, miners)

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.sc: A factory manager wants to reduce worker exposure to a hazardous solvent used in a manufacturing process.
tk: Name the five levels of the hierarchy of controls, in order of preference from most to least effective.
Give an example of an 'elimination' control applicable to this scenario.
Give an example of a 'personal protective equipment' control applicable to this scenario.
Explain why personal protective equipment is considered the least preferred control measure.
ck: Lists elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, and personal protective equipment
States replacing the hazardous solvent with a non-hazardous or less hazardous alternative
States use of respirators, gloves, or protective clothing
Explains it relies on correct and consistent worker compliance and does not remove the hazard itself

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.sc: A rapidly growing urban municipality is developing a solid waste management plan and must decide on a hierarchy of preferred waste management strategies.
tk: Name the generally preferred hierarchy of solid waste management strategies, from most to least preferred.
State why open dumping is considered the least acceptable disposal method from a public health standpoint.
Name the appropriate segregation category and disposal method required for biomedical (hospital) waste, distinct from general municipal waste.
Name one health risk to waste handlers associated with improper segregation of sharps waste.
ck: States reduction/recycling preferred over treatment and controlled/sanitary disposal, with open dumping least preferred
States open dumping risks contamination of water/soil, vector breeding, and disease transmission
States biomedical waste requires separate segregation (e.g., color-coded bags) and specific treatment such as autoclaving or incineration
States risk of needlestick injury and transmission of bloodborne pathogens (e.g., HIV, hepatitis B/C)

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.sc: A woman dies from postpartum hemorrhage after a home delivery, having experienced a long delay in reaching a hospital due to lack of transport, following an even longer delay by the family in deciding to seek care.
tk: Apply the 'three delays model' to identify which delays are illustrated in this case.
Name the most common direct cause of maternal mortality illustrated in this scenario.
Name the key evidence-based strategy for reducing this specific complication during the third stage of labor.
Name one health system-level intervention that could reduce the second delay (reaching a facility) in similar rural settings.
ck: Identifies the first delay (deciding to seek care) and second delay (reaching a facility)
Names postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony
Names active management of the third stage of labor with a uterotonic (e.g., oxytocin)
States improving transport/referral systems (e.g., emergency transport schemes, maternity waiting homes)

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.t: Antenatal Care and Risk Screening Station
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.sc: A pregnant woman attends her first antenatal visit at 10 weeks gestation, and the healthcare provider conducts a series of assessments and counseling as per WHO guidelines.
tk: State the minimum number of antenatal contacts currently recommended by WHO for a normal pregnancy.
Name two key screening/preventive interventions typically offered at antenatal visits.
State the primary purpose of antenatal care in terms of pregnancy outcomes.
Name the tool used during labor to graphically monitor progress and detect prolonged/obstructed labor early.
ck: States a minimum of eight contacts
States interventions such as blood pressure monitoring, hemoglobin/anemia screening, tetanus toxoid vaccination, or HIV/syphilis screening
States early identification and management of pregnancy-related risk factors and complications
Names the partograph

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.sc: A woman who has just delivered her third child wishes to space her next pregnancy by at least 2-3 years and asks about contraceptive options while breastfeeding.
tk: Name the minimum recommended inter-pregnancy interval to optimize maternal and child health outcomes.
Name one contraceptive method generally considered compatible with breastfeeding.
Explain how family planning contributes to reducing maternal mortality at a population level.
Define 'unmet need for family planning' as it would apply to a woman in a similar situation who is not using any method despite wanting to delay pregnancy.
ck: States at least 2 years between pregnancies
Names progestin-only methods (e.g., progestin-only pills, injectable, implant) or the lactational amenorrhea method/copper IUD as compatible options
Explains it reduces the cumulative number of pregnancies (and associated risk exposure) a woman experiences over her lifetime
Defines unmet need as a fecund, sexually active woman who wants to delay/avoid pregnancy but is not using contraception

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.sc: A district health department is conducting an assessment of its local health system's performance using the WHO health systems framework.
tk: Name the six building blocks of a health system as defined by WHO.
Give an example of an indicator that could be used to assess the 'health workforce' building block.
Explain the concept of universal health coverage as a health system goal.
Name one financing mechanism that helps protect households from catastrophic health expenditure.
ck: Names service delivery, health workforce, health information systems, medical products/technologies, financing, and leadership/governance
States an indicator such as health worker density per population or workforce distribution/training levels
Explains ensuring all people receive needed quality health services without financial hardship
Names social/national health insurance or pooled risk financing mechanisms
